profiles.meeting_scenario: A cross-functional design review meeting at an international health-policy nonprofit preparing a comparative policy brief and submission template for digital therapeutics (DTx) manufacturers seeking reimbursement across six countries: Canada, USA, UK, Germany, France, and Australia. The team is reviewing a draft framework that adapts existing health technology assessment (HTA) evidence expectations using the UK NICE evidence standards framework as the anchor and proposes a 'minimum cross-country submission package' for markets without DTx-specific guidance. The agenda is to assess whether the draft comparison table, evidence requirements, and approval recommendations are ready for circulation to external reviewers. The expected outcome is a decision on whether the draft is review-ready with a short list of edits, not a full rewrite.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: comparative effectiveness, reimbursement dossiers, economic evaluation frameworks
members.background: Trained as a health economist, Maya previously worked on oncology and medical device appraisals for a national assessment body and now leads methodological design for international evidence frameworks.
members.private_state: She wants the draft approved today so the nonprofit can stay on schedule for an expert roundtable, but she is also trying to preserve methodological rigor by avoiding claims that overstate country readiness for DTx reimbursement.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says the framework is 'cross-country,' it means a mapping of current HTA expectations by jurisdiction, even if several countries only have implicit or analog pathways rather than explicit DTx guidance.

A 'budget impact analysis' in this draft means a payer-facing one-year to three-year affordability estimate at national or major regional reimbursement scale, not a clinic-level implementation budget.

If a section is labeled 'submission-ready,' it only needs to be sufficiently coherent for external policy expert review, with placeholder caveats acceptable so long as methodological caveats are already embedded in footnotes.
Using NICE as the anchor is acceptable as long as the draft clearly distinguishes where other countries lack formal DTx-specific guidance and instead rely on general HTA analogies.

members.name: Alex Romero
members.expertise: digital therapeutics adoption, provider implementation, market access communications
members.background: Alex has led partnerships with hospital systems and DTx startups, focusing on scaling digital care programs and translating policy requirements into operational guidance for product teams.
members.private_state: He wants the document to feel practical and immediately usable by DTx companies and provider networks, and he is worried that too many caveats will make the brief seem indecisive or less valuable to stakeholders.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says the framework is 'cross-country,' it should function as a usable submission playbook for all six countries, even where formal guidance is absent, by inferring likely reviewer expectations from adjacent pathways.

A 'budget impact analysis' should capture what adoption will cost the implementing health system or provider group in practice, including onboarding, clinician training, and integration burdens, because that is what shapes real uptake.
If a section is called 'submission-ready,' it should be polished enough that a manufacturer or policy lead could adapt it with minimal interpretation and no unresolved placeholders.

Referring to the 'NICE framework' naturally includes the broader practical lessons from NICE's digital health evidence standards and surrounding implementation-oriented materials, not just the single formal evidence standards document.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both endorse making the draft a 'cross-country framework' for the six-country comparison.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 understands this as a jurisdictional comparison that documents what each country formally requires or plausibly accepts, with explicit acknowledgment that five countries lack DTx-specific guidance.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 understands this as a practical template that fills those gaps and gives users a near-operational route for submitting in all six countries, even if some country-specific expectations must be inferred.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both views sound mutually supportive because both favor broad international usefulness; the divergence concerns the boundary between descriptive mapping and prescriptive playbook design, which feels like an implementation detail rather than a core disagreement.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree every economic analysis level should include a 'budget impact analysis.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the standard payer-perspective affordability estimate used in HTA submissions, typically focused on reimbursement budgets over a defined horizon.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a broader adoption-cost model that includes provider onboarding, workflow redesign, training, and integration costs because those drive whether DTx is actually affordable in practice.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is standard and both are familiar with it, so neither expects that the other is extending or narrowing the term; the meeting is a design review, so they treat the phrase as already settled vocabulary.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the NICE framework' as the anchor for the draft.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring specifically to NICE's formal evidence standards framework that separates digital health technologies by evidence and economic-analysis levels.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the broader set of NICE-related digital evaluation materials and implementation-oriented lessons that he has previously used in partnership discussions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: NICE is the only country in the review with identifiable DTx/DHT guidance, so saying 'the NICE framework' feels unambiguous; both assume the other is invoking the same bundle of documents because the shorthand is common in interdisciplinary teams.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the draft is 'review-ready' for external circulation next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes review-ready means the logic, caveats, and table structure are stable enough for expert review even if wording and examples still need refinement.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes review-ready means externally presentable and practically actionable, with cleaned-up language, filled examples, and no visible placeholders that could confuse stakeholders.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design reviews, teams routinely say a draft is 'ready for review' without restating whether they mean concept review or polished circulation draft; both assume their standard is the obvious one for this stage.

I just need to make sure we are not overstating readiness in countries that do not actually have formal DTx reimbursement guidance.
